title: Time-of-Use Electricity Rates Explained (2026)
h1: Time-of-use electricity rates explained: peak vs. off-peak pricing
desc: Time-of-use electricity rates charge more at peak hours and less off-peak. See two worked examples, who benefits, and Texas vs. regulated utility rules.
lede: Time-of-use electricity rates charge different prices for electricity depending on when you use it, typically higher during late-afternoon and evening peak hours and lower overnight or on weekends. These plans help you save money if you can shift usage like laundry, dishwashing, or EV charging to off-peak hours, but they can raise your bill if most of your usage happens during peak times.
body:
What time-of-use electricity rates actually mean

A time-of-use (TOU) rate splits your day into pricing windows instead of charging one flat cents-per-kWh price. You pay more for electricity during peak hours, usually late afternoon through evening when demand on the grid is highest, and less during off-peak hours overnight, early morning, or on weekends. Some plans add a middle shoulder price too.

The idea behind TOU pricing is simple: electricity is more expensive to produce and deliver when everyone wants it at once. Utilities and retail electric providers pass some of that cost difference on to you, and reward you for using power when the grid has spare capacity.

How peak and off-peak hours are typically set

Peak windows vary by utility and by season, but most residential TOU plans in the U.S. set peak hours somewhere between 2 p.m. and 9 p.m. on weekdays, often narrowing to the most expensive stretch between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. in summer, when air conditioning load is highest. Weekends and major holidays are usually treated as off-peak all day. Some plans also widen the peak window in winter to cover early-morning heating demand.

Before you sign up for any TOU plan, read its rate disclosure for the exact hours and prices. If you're in Texas, every plan is required to publish an Electricity Facts Label showing average prices at 500, 1,000 and 2,000 kWh; see how to read an Electricity Facts Label to find the numbers that matter for your usage.

Who actually benefits from time-of-use rates

TOU rates are not automatically a good deal. You come out ahead only if you can move a meaningful share of your usage out of the peak window. You're a good candidate if:

  • You charge an electric vehicle at home and can set it to charge after midnight instead of right after work.
  • You run the dishwasher, washer, and dryer in the evening and could shift them to late night or early morning.
  • You have a pool pump, water heater, or smart thermostat that can be scheduled.
  • You work from home with flexible hours, or you're often out of the house during the 4-8 p.m. peak.

You're a poor candidate if your household is busiest exactly during peak hours, for example a family that cooks dinner, runs the AC, and does homework between 5 and 9 p.m. with no flexibility. For that pattern, a flat-rate plan may cost less. If you're unsure which category you fall into, compare the trade-offs in fixed vs. variable electricity rates before committing to a time-based plan.

Worked example 1: a small apartment

Say a one-bedroom apartment uses 600 kWh in a summer month. On a flat plan at the U.S. average residential rate of 18.34 cents/kWh, the energy cost is:

600 kWh × $0.1834 = $110.04

Now compare a sample TOU plan with a peak rate of 34 cents/kWh from 4-9 p.m. and an off-peak rate of 10 cents/kWh the rest of the day. If the renter's normal routine puts 150 kWh in that peak window (cooking, AC, lights) and 450 kWh off-peak:

(150 × $0.34) + (450 × $0.10) = $51.00 + $45.00 = $96.00

That's already $14.04 cheaper than the flat plan, just from the apartment's natural usage pattern. Now suppose the renter moves laundry and dishwasher loads (about 50 kWh) from the evening peak to after 9 p.m., trimming peak usage to 100 kWh and pushing off-peak to 500 kWh:

(100 × $0.34) + (500 × $0.10) = $34.00 + $50.00 = $84.00

Shifting just 50 kWh saved another $12, for total savings of $26.04 a month compared with the flat-rate plan, about 24% off the energy charge. For context on what's typical in a unit this size, see how many kWh a house uses per month.

Worked example 2: a large house with an EV

Now take a larger home using 2,000 kWh in a month, including an electric vehicle. On a flat plan at the Texas average rate of 15.94 cents/kWh:

2,000 kWh × $0.1594 = $318.80

Say this household's TOU plan charges 32 cents/kWh from 3-7 p.m. weekdays and 9 cents/kWh at all other times. Before changing any habits, the home uses 500 kWh during peak (AC cycling, dinner, EV plugged in right after work) and 1,500 kWh off-peak:

(500 × $0.32) + (1,500 × $0.09) = $160.00 + $135.00 = $295.00

That's already $23.80 less than the flat plan before any behavior change. Now the homeowner sets the EV charger on a delay so the car's roughly 300 kWh of monthly charging happens after 11 p.m. instead of right after work. Peak usage drops to 200 kWh and off-peak rises to 1,800 kWh:

(200 × $0.32) + (1,800 × $0.09) = $64.00 + $162.00 = $226.00

Delaying the EV charge alone cut the bill by another $69, for total savings of $92.80 a month versus the flat plan, about 29% off the energy charge. For a deeper look at charging costs, see how much it costs to charge an EV at home.

A simple break-even rule before you switch

You don't need a spreadsheet to decide if TOU makes sense. Use this rule of thumb: estimate what share of your kWh currently falls in the plan's peak window. If that share is below roughly 30-35% of your total usage, and you can shift even a small slice of it further down, a TOU plan with a meaningful peak-to-off-peak spread (roughly 2x or more, like 30 cents versus 10-12 cents) will usually beat a flat rate. If your peak-window share is above 40-45% and inflexible, skip it and look at what counts as a good price per kWh for a flat-rate benchmark instead.

Regulated utility TOU plans vs. Texas retail TOU plans

In states with a regulated, single utility, like most of the Southeast and Mountain West, time-of-use rates are offered directly by that utility as an opt-in or sometimes default schedule, and the peak hours and prices are filed with the state regulator.

In deregulated states, including Texas, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, New York, New Jersey, Maryland, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and the District of Columbia, you choose a TOU plan from a competitive retail electric provider rather than the wires utility. In Texas specifically, the company delivering power to your home (like Oncor, CenterPoint Energy, AEP Texas, or Texas-New Mexico Power) is separate from the retail provider that sets your energy price, and that delivery company charges its own per-kWh and monthly fee on top of whatever energy rate you pick. See Texas TDU delivery charges for exact figures by area. Wholesale-indexed residential plans, where your rate tracks the real-time wholesale market directly, were banned in Texas after Winter Storm Uri in 2021, so any TOU plan you see today uses fixed time-block pricing set by the retail provider, not live wholesale prices.

Because Texas is deregulated, you can shop among multiple TOU offers rather than being stuck with one utility schedule. Before switching, confirm the exact peak hours on the Electricity Facts Label, since one provider's "peak" might be 1-6 p.m. and another's might be 5-9 p.m., which changes whether your household benefits at all.

How rate structures compare across states

Your starting flat rate matters too, since it's the baseline you're measuring TOU savings against. Here's how average residential rates compare in several deregulated states where TOU retail plans are common:

StateAverage rate (cents/kWh)Market type
Texas15.94Deregulated
Ohio19.19Deregulated
Illinois19.89Deregulated
Pennsylvania21.73Deregulated
Maryland21.84Deregulated
New Jersey24.95Deregulated
Connecticut24.32Deregulated
New York29.49Deregulated
Massachusetts29.61Deregulated

A wide peak-to-off-peak spread saves you more in a high-rate state like Massachusetts or New York than in a lower-rate state like Texas or Ohio, simply because there's more room between the peak price and the off-peak price. Check your state's current average on our state-by-state rate comparison before estimating savings.

Practical ways to shift load without disrupting your routine

You don't need to overhaul your life to benefit from TOU pricing. A few changes move real kWh out of peak hours:

  • Set your dishwasher and washing machine to run on a delay timer, starting after 9 or 10 p.m.
  • Pre-cool your house 1-2 degrees before peak hours start, then let the thermostat drift up during the peak window, as outlined in 15 tips to lower your electric bill in summer.
  • Charge your EV on a timer set for after midnight rather than when you plug in after work.
  • Run the pool pump and water heater on off-peak schedules if they have smart or mechanical timers.
  • Check your real usage pattern first using a smart meter portal; in Texas, see Smart Meter Texas: how to see your usage to find out exactly how many kWh you use by hour before you commit to a TOU plan.

What to do next

Pull your last 2-3 months of hourly usage data if your utility or smart meter portal provides it, and calculate what share falls in a candidate plan's peak window. Run the math the way we did above using your actual kWh split, not just averages. If the numbers favor a TOU plan and you're in a deregulated state, compare current offers side by side, checking the exact peak hours on the Electricity Facts Label, not just the headline rate. If you're in Texas and ready to shop, start with our electricity rate comparison tool to see TOU and flat-rate plans available at your address.
faq: Do time-of-use rates save everyone money?

No. They only save money if a meaningful share of your usage happens off-peak, or if you can shift usage like laundry or EV charging away from the peak window. Households that use most of their electricity during peak hours often pay more on a TOU plan than on a flat rate.
What hours are usually considered peak for electricity?

Most residential TOU plans set peak hours somewhere between 2 p.m. and 9 p.m. on weekdays, with the highest prices often concentrated between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. in summer. Exact hours vary by utility or retail provider, so always check the plan's rate disclosure.
Are time-of-use rates different in Texas than other states?

Yes. In Texas you choose a TOU plan from a competitive retail provider, and a separate delivery company charges its own per-kWh and monthly fee on top. Wholesale-indexed residential plans were banned in Texas after Winter Storm Uri in 2021, so Texas TOU plans use fixed time-block pricing, not live wholesale prices.
How do I know if I use more electricity on-peak or off-peak?

Check your utility's smart meter portal or your provider's usage history, which usually breaks down kWh by hour or by time block. In Texas, Smart Meter Texas lets you view your interval usage directly so you can calculate your peak-hours percentage before switching plans.
